title: Safari Net Rates, Explained for Travel Agents Who Sell East Africa
meta_title: Safari Net Rates and Commission for Travel Agents
meta_description: How safari net rates work for travel agents: net vs commissionable, park fees at cost, seasons, markup maths and deposits across East Africa.
excerpt: A plain guide to safari net rates for travel agents and tour operators: net vs commissionable pricing, pass-through park fees, seasonality, markup and deposit terms in East Africa.
content:
Safari net rates for travel agents are the trade prices a ground handler charges before you add your own markup, so you set the final selling price yourself. A commissionable rate works the other way round: the client price is fixed and you earn a percentage of it. Park fees and gorilla permits usually pass through at cost.

The difficulty is that a safari quote mixes items with very different rules. Lodge rooms are contracted with margin built in, government fees carry none, permits are non-refundable, and prices shift by season. This guide explains how safari net rates are built in Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda and Rwanda, how to price them safely and what to ask before you sign. It is the framework we use when our safari DMC service for travel agents and tour leaders prepares trade quotes from Nairobi.

Quick Facts

  • Net rate: Trade price from the ground handler; you add your markup and set the client price
  • Commissionable rate: Fixed client price; you earn an agreed percentage
  • Pass-through items: Park and conservancy fees, gorilla and chimpanzee permits, government levies and entry insurance
  • Biggest seasonal swing: Masai Mara reserve fee: US$100 per adult per day January-June, US$200 July-December (checked October 2026)
  • Pricing currency: Most East African safari rates are quoted in US dollars
  • Least flexible item: Gorilla permits: paid in full at booking and non-refundable in Rwanda
  • Always confirm: Rate validity dates, deposit schedule and how fee changes are passed on

What Are Safari Net Rates?

Safari net rates are the prices a local ground handler charges a travel agent or tour operator for a complete programme, before the agent adds a markup. The ground handler's own costs and margin are already inside the figure, so the net price is what you pay and the rest is yours.

Safari net rates are the standard model for tailor-made trips because no two itineraries are the same. A family of five in the Masai Mara in August and a pair of honeymooners in Tarangire in May need completely different quotes, and the agent needs freedom to price each one for its own market. Commissionable pricing still exists, but it suits fixed products more than private safaris.

Net, commissionable, rack and static tour operator rates compared

The words on a rate sheet matter, because the same lodge night can appear at three different prices depending on who is reading. The table below sets out the four terms you will meet most often.

Rate typeWho sets the client priceHow the agent earns
Net rateThe agentThe markup the agent adds on top
Commissionable rateThe supplierAn agreed percentage of the fixed price
Rack rateThe lodge (public price)Nothing on its own; it is the benchmark direct guests pay
STO rateThe lodge, for the trade onlyThe gap between STO and the price the agent packages and sells

STO stands for static tour operator. Lodges publish it to the trade at a reduction on the rack rate, on the understanding that it is sold inside a package and never shown publicly. When a ground handler quotes you safari net rates, its lodge costs are usually STO or contracted rates, which is why its package can still be priced competitively after your markup.

What Goes Into a Net Safari Quote?

A quote built on safari net rates is the sum of a few cost blocks: accommodation, the vehicle and driver-guide, park and conservancy fees, transfers and internal flights, and optional activities. Asking for each block as its own line is the single best protection against surprises, because each one behaves differently when dates or numbers change.

Accommodation is normally the largest block and the one with margin built in at every level. The vehicle is charged per day and is shared by everyone in it, so the price per person falls as the group grows, up to the seats available. Flights are priced per seat, with luggage limits on light aircraft that affect what your clients can pack.

Pass-through costs that carry no ground handler margin

Government fees are usually passed through at cost inside safari net rates. They are set by bodies such as the Kenya Wildlife Service, Tanzania National Parks, the Uganda Wildlife Authority and the Rwanda Development Board, and the ground handler cannot discount them. Our Kenya park fees guide and Tanzania park fees guide list the full tariffs.

FeeCurrent figureWhy it matters for agents
Masai Mara reserve feeUS$100 per adult per day January-June, US$200 July-December (checked October 2026)Doubles in peak season, so a June quote and a July quote differ sharply
Amboseli and Lake Nakuru (KWS)US$90 per adult per 24 hours (checked October 2026)Paid cashless through eCitizen; your ground handler pays it on your behalf
Serengeti (TANAPA)US$82.60 per adult per 24 hours in high season, US$70.80 from 15 March to 15 May (checked October 2026)Includes Tanzania's 18% VAT; changes with the low-season window
Ngorongoro CraterUS$295 per vehicle for each crater descent (checked October 2026)A per-vehicle charge, so it costs less per person in a full vehicle
Rwanda gorilla permitUS$1,500 per person per trek (checked October 2026)Paid in full at booking and non-refundable
Tanzania inbound travel insuranceUS$44 per adult, mandatory since 1 October 2026 (checked November 2026)Make clear in your quote who buys it

Uganda gorilla permits are sold through the Uganda Wildlife Authority, and the price is set by the date of the trek rather than the date of purchase. Reports of a change for treks from January 2027 vary, so confirm the current tariff with the authority before quoting. Our Rwanda gorilla permit guide covers booking rules on the Rwanda side. All the fee figures above change, so please confirm them before you book.

How Does Seasonality Change Your Trade Prices?

Seasonality changes safari net rates in two ways: lodges charge more in peak months, and some government fees rise at the same time. In Kenya and northern Tanzania the expensive months are broadly July to October and the Christmas and New Year weeks, while April and May bring the lowest prices and some camp closures.

Lodge season dates behind safari net rates are not standard, so two camps in the same reserve can switch from low to high season a fortnight apart. When a trip crosses a season boundary, safari net rates should price each night at its own season rate rather than averaging. Ask to see this on the quote, especially for itineraries that start in late June or end in early November.

Period (Kenya and northern Tanzania)What usually happens to net ratesSelling point for clients
January to MarchMid-range pricing at many campsDry weather and calving season in the southern Serengeti
April to MayLowest rates; some camps closeGreen landscapes, fewer vehicles, lower Serengeti fees from 15 March to 15 May
JuneRates rising; Mara fee still at the lower levelEarly migration movement in the western Serengeti
July to OctoberPeak rates and the higher Mara feeMigration in the Masai Mara and river crossings
November to mid-DecemberShoulder pricing at many campsShort rains, quieter parks, good value
Late December to early JanuaryFestive supplements at many lodgesHoliday demand; book early

Rwanda adds a twist: the gorilla permit drops by 30% from November to May for visitors who also stay two nights in Akagera or Nyungwe national parks, according to the Rwanda Development Board (checked October 2026). That can make a longer Rwanda itinerary cheaper per gorilla trek than a short one, which is worth showing clients.

How Much Markup Should You Add to Safari Net Rates?

No single markup is right for safari net rates. It has to cover your sales time, card or bank charges, currency movement, cancellation risk and profit. Agents often apply a lower markup to high-value permits and park fees, so the selling price stays credible next to official published fees.

Be careful with the arithmetic. Markup is calculated on the net price; margin is measured on the selling price. As a purely illustrative example, a programme with a net price of US$1,000 per person sold with a 20% markup costs the client US$1,200, but your margin is US$200 of US$1,200, or about 16.7%. Mixing the two terms when working with safari net rates is one of the most common reasons agents earn less than they planned.

Pricing groups from safari net rates

Group pricing with safari net rates follows the shared costs. Vehicles, guides and some transfers are divided by the number of travellers, so per-person prices fall as you fill seats, while lodge nights, park fees and permits stay per person. Ask for safari net rates at several group sizes, say 2, 4, 6 and 12, plus single supplements, so you can quote confidently if numbers change. Deposits, Payment Terms and Cancellations

Safari payments run in a chain: the lodge asks the ground handler for a deposit, the ground handler asks you, and you ask your client. The golden rule is that your client's deposit and balance must reach you before each supplier deadline, never after it, or you end up funding the trip from your own account.

Under most safari net rates contracts, lodges request a deposit when a booking is confirmed and the balance some weeks before arrival, with stricter terms in peak season and over Christmas. Gorilla permits are usually paid in full at booking because the authorities require it. Each supplier sets its own terms, so ask your ground handler for one payment schedule that lists every deadline in date order.

Cancellation rules to mirror in your own terms

Cancellation charges on safari net rates usually rise as the travel date gets closer, and some items are lost entirely once paid. Rwanda gorilla permits are non-refundable and rescheduling costs 20% of the permit fee (checked October 2026). Build these rules into your own client terms, and recommend that every traveller buys travel insurance with cancellation cover from the day they pay a deposit.

Questions to Ask Before You Accept a Safari Rate Sheet

The best time to settle how safari net rates work is before your first booking, not when a client is waiting. These are the questions we would want answered in your seat, and they sit well alongside the checklists in our guide to choosing a Kenya safari DMC and our Tanzania ground handler guide.

  • Are these safari net rates or commissionable rates, and in which currency?
  • Which items are passed through at cost, and are they shown as separate lines?
  • What are the validity dates, and what happens if a park fee rises mid-year?
  • Are lodge nights priced at each night's own season rate across season boundaries?
  • What are the deposit, balance and cancellation deadlines for each supplier?
  • What is included in the vehicle price: fuel, guide fees, water, park entry for the vehicle?
  • How are bank charges handled, and who pays them on each transfer?
  • Who answers the phone at night if a flight is cancelled or a client falls ill?

If you sell Kenya and Tanzania together, also ask how the vehicle handover at the border is priced, since Kenyan safari vehicles cannot operate inside Tanzania's parks. Insider Tips

  • Quote with an expiry date: Give clients a price that is valid for a fixed number of days, because lodge availability and fees move
  • Price permits first: Check gorilla permit availability before you send a quote that depends on a specific date
  • Separate peak-season fees: Show the Masai Mara fee as its own line so clients understand why July costs more than June
  • Ask for group bands: Request net prices for several group sizes at the start, not after numbers change
  • Watch currency: Agree whether you pay in US dollars and who carries the bank charges on each transfer
  • Keep it in writing: Save every rate sheet, payment schedule and change of terms in one file per booking

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between net and commissionable safari rates?

A net safari rate is the trade price you pay the ground handler, and you decide the selling price by adding your own markup. A commissionable rate comes with a fixed client price, and you earn an agreed percentage of it. Net rates give the agent pricing control; commissionable rates keep one client price everywhere.

Are park fees included in safari net rates?

Park fees are usually included in safari net rates as a separate line passed through at cost, with no margin from the ground handler. Fees such as the Masai Mara reserve fee or Rwanda's gorilla permit are set by government authorities and change by season or by year, so ask for them itemised and check whether your markup applies to them.

How much markup do travel agents add to safari net rates?

There is no fixed markup on safari net rates; each agent sets one that covers its sales costs, card and bank charges, currency risk and profit. Remember that markup and margin are different: a 20% markup on a net price gives a margin of about 16.7% of the selling price. Many agents apply a lower markup to permits and park fees than to accommodation.

When do safari lodges and ground handlers ask for deposits?

Safari deposits are normally requested when a booking is confirmed, with the balance due some weeks before arrival, but every lodge and ground handler sets its own terms. Gorilla permits are usually paid in full at booking. Ask for the full payment schedule in writing and set your client terms so their money reaches you before each supplier deadline.

How long are safari net rates valid?

Safari net rates are usually issued for a set period, often a calendar year or a season, and park fees can change within that period if an authority publishes a new tariff. Check the validity dates on every rate sheet, ask how mid-year fee increases are handled, and quote clients with a clear expiry date.

Final Thoughts

Safari net rates give you control of your own pricing, but only when every line is clear: lodge costs with margin, government fees at cost, seasons priced night by night and payment deadlines in writing. Get those right and your markup stays yours.
